entries.3c0d1c1e4d1a55680d503cc18bca2f303d522560: <div sID="gen17962" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="35" osisID="Jer.35" sID="Jer.35"/> <div eID="gen17962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17963" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17964" type="x-p"/> A variety of methods is tried, and every stone turned, to awaken the Jews to a sense of their sin and to bring them to repentance and reformation. The scope and tendency of many of the prophet's sermons was to frighten them out of their disobedience, by setting before them what would be the end thereof if they persisted in it. The scope of this sermon, in this chapter, is to shame them out of their disobedience if they had any sense of honour left in them for a discourse of this nature to fasten upon. I. He sets before them the obedience of the family of the Rechabites to the commands which were left them by Jonadab their ancestor, and how they persevered in that obedience and would not be tempted from it, <reference osisRef="Jer.35.1-Jer.35.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. With this he aggravates the disobedience of the Jews to God and their contempt of his precepts, <reference osisRef="Jer.35.12-Jer.35.15">ver. 12-15</reference>. III. He foretels the judgments of God upon the Jews for their impious disobedience to God, <reference osisRef="Jer.35.16-Jer.35.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>. IV. He assures the Rechabites of the blessing of God upon them for their pious obedience to their father, <reference osisRef="Jer.35.18-Jer.35.19">ver. 18, 19</reference>.
entries.7961820f71fe7cc5ecf0ed2803669bb4ed132bd4: <div eID="gen17964" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17963" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Case of the Rechabites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 607.)</title> <div sID="gen17965" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word which came unto Jeremiah from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Go unto the house of the Rechabites, and speak unto them, and bring them into the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , into one of the chambers, and give them wine to drink. <hi type="super">3</hi> Then I took Jaazaniah the son of Jeremiah, the son of Habaziniah, and his brethren, and all his sons, and the whole house of the Rechabites; <hi type="super">4</hi> And I brought them into the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , into the chamber of the sons of Hanan, the son of Igdaliah, a man of God, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> by the chamber of the princes, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> above the chamber of Maaseiah the son of Shallum, the keeper of the door: <hi type="super">5</hi> And I set before the sons of the house of the Rechabites pots full of wine, and cups, and I said unto them, Drink ye wine. <hi type="super">6</hi> But they said, We will drink no wine: for Jonadab the son of Rechab our father commanded us, saying, Ye shall drink no wine, <hi type="italic">neither ye,</hi> nor your sons for ever: <hi type="super">7</hi> Neither shall ye build house, nor sow seed, nor plant vineyard, nor have <hi type="italic">any:</hi> but all your days ye shall dwell in tents; that ye may live many days in the land where ye <hi type="italic">be</hi> strangers. <hi type="super">8</hi> Thus have we obeyed the voice of Jonadab the son of Rechab our father in all that he hath charged us, to drink no wine all our days, we, our wives, our sons, nor our daughters; <hi type="super">9</hi> Nor to build houses for us to dwell in: neither have we vineyard, nor field, nor seed: <hi type="super">10</hi> But we have dwelt in tents, and have obeyed, and done according to all that Jonadab our father commanded us. <hi type="super">11</hi> But it came to pass, when Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon came up into the land, that we said, Come, and let us go to Jerusalem for fear of the army of the Chaldeans, and for fear of the army of the Syrians: so we dwell at Jerusalem. <div eID="gen17965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17966" type="x-p"/> This chapter is of an earlier date than many of those before; for what is contained in it was said and done <hi type="italic">in the days of Jehoiakim</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.1">v. 1</reference>); but then it must be in the latter part of his reign, for it was after the king of Babylon with his army <hi type="italic">came up into the land</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.11">v. 11</reference>), which seems to refer to the invasion mentioned <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.2">2 Kings xxiv. 2</reference>, which was upon occasion of Jehoiakim's rebelling against Nebuchadnezzar. After the judgments of God had broken in upon this rebellious people he continued to deal with them by his prophets to turn them from sin, that his wrath might turn away from the. For this purpose Jeremiah sets before them the example of the Rechabites, a family that kept distinct by themselves and were no more numbered with the families of Israel than they with the nations. They were originally Kenites, as appears <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.55">1 Chron. ii. 55</reference>, <hi type="italic">These are the Kenites that came out of Hemath, the father of the house of Rechab.</hi> The Kenites, at least those of them that gained a settlement in the land of Israel, were of the posterity of Hobab, Moses's father-in-law, <reference osisRef="Judg.1.16">Judg. i. 16</reference>. We find them separated from the Amalekites, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.6">1 Sam. xv. 6</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Judg.4.17">Judg. iv. 17</reference>. One family of these Kenites had their denomination from Rechab. His son, or a lineal descendant from him, was Jonadab, a man famous in his time for wisdom and piety. He flourished in the days of Jehu, king of Israel, nearly 300 years before this; for there we find him courted by that rising prince, when he affected to appear zealous for God (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.15-2Kgs.10.16">2 Kings x. 15, 16</reference>), which he thought nothing more likely to confirm people in the opinion of than to have so good a man as Jonadab ride in the chariot with him. Now here we are told, <div eID="gen17966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17967" type="x-p"/> I. What the rules of living were which Jonadab, probably by his last will and testament, in writing, and duly executed, charged his children, and his posterity after him throughout all generations, religiously to observe; and we have reason to think that they were such as he himself had all his days observed. <div eID="gen17967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17968" type="x-p"/> 1. They were comprised in two remarkable precepts:—(1.) He forbade them to <hi type="italic">drink wine,</hi> according to the law of the Nazarites. Wine is indeed given to <hi type="italic">make glad the heart</hi> of man and we are allowed the sober and moderate use of it; but we are so apt to abuse it and get hurt by it, and a good man, who has his heart made continually glad with the <hi type="italic">light of God's countenance,</hi> has so little need of it for that purpose (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.6-Ps.4.7">Ps. iv. 6, 7</reference>), that it is a commendable piece of self-denial either not to use it at all or very sparingly and medicinally, as Timothy used it, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.23">1 Tim. v. 23</reference>. (2.) He appointed them to <hi type="italic">dwell in tents,</hi> and not to build houses, nor purchase lands, nor rent or occupy either, <reference osisRef="Jer.35.7">v. 7</reference>. This was an instance of strictness and mortification beyond what the Nazarenes were obliged to. Tents were mean dwellings, so that this would teach them to be humble; they were cold dwellings, so that this would teach them to be hardy and not to indulge the body; they were movable dwellings, so that this would teach them not to think of settling or taking root any where in this world. They must dwell in tents <hi type="italic">all their days.</hi> They must from the beginning thus accustom themselves to endure hardness, and then it would be no difficulty to them, no, not under the decays of old age. Now, <div eID="gen17968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17969" type="x-p"/> 2. Why did Jonadab prescribe these rules of living to his posterity? It was not merely to show his authority, and to exercise a dominion over them, by imposing upon them what he thought fit; but it was to show his wisdom, and the real concern he had for their welfare, by recommending to them what he knew would be beneficial to them, yet not tying them by any oath or vow, or under any penalty, to observe these rules, but only advising them to conform to this discipline as far as they found it for edification, yet to be dispensed with in any case of necessity, as here, <reference osisRef="Jer.35.11">v. 11</reference>. He prescribed these rules to them, (1.) That they might preserve the ancient character of their family, which, however looked upon by some with contempt, he thought its real reputation. His ancestors had addicted themselves to a pastoral life (<reference osisRef="Exod.2.16">Exod. ii. 16</reference>), and he would have his posterity keep to it, and not degenerate from it, as Israel had done, who originally were shepherds and dwelt in tents, <reference osisRef="Gen.46.34">Gen. xlvi. 34</reference>. Note, We ought not to be ashamed of the honest employments of our ancestors, though they were but mean. (2.) That they might comport with their lot and bring their mind to their condition. Moses had put them in hopes that they should be naturalized (<reference osisRef="Num.10.32">Num. x. 32</reference>); but, it seems they were not; they were still <hi type="italic">strangers in the land</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.7">v. 7</reference>), had no inheritance in it, and therefore must live by their employments, which was a good reason why they should accustom themselves to hard fare and hard lodging; for strangers, such as they were, must not expect to live as the landed men, so plentifully and delicately. Note, It is our wisdom and duty to accommodate ourselves to our place and rank, and not aim to live above it. What has been the lot of our fathers why may we not be content that it should be our lot, and live according to it? <hi type="italic">Mind not high things.</hi> (3.) That they might not be envied and disturbed by their neighbours among whom they lived. If they that were strangers should live great, raise estates, and fare sumptuously, the natives would grudge them their abundance, and have a jealous eye upon them, as the Philistines had upon Isaac (<reference osisRef="Gen.26.14">Gen. xxvi. 14</reference>), and would seek occasions to quarrel with them and do them a mischief; therefore he thought it would be their prudence to keep low, for that would be the way to continue long-to live meanly, that they might <hi type="italic">live many days in the land where they were strangers.</hi> Note, Humility and contentment in obscurity are often the best policy and men's surest protection. (4.) That they might be armed against temptations to luxury and sensuality, the prevailing sin of the age and place they lived in. Jonadab saw a general corruption of manners; the drunkards of Ephraim abounded, and he was afraid lest his children should be debauched and ruined by them; and therefore he obliged them to live by themselves, retired in the country; and, that they might not run into any unlawful pleasures, to deny themselves the use even of lawful delights. They must be very sober, and temperate, and abstemious, which would contribute to the health both of mind and body, and to their living many days, and easy ones, and such as they might reflect upon with comfort <hi type="italic">in the land where they were strangers.</hi> Note, The consideration of this, that we are strangers and pilgrims, should oblige us to abstain from all fleshly lusts, to live above the things of sense, and look upon them with a generous and gracious contempt. (5.) That they might be prepared for times of trouble and calamity. Jonadab might, without a spirit of prophecy, foresee the destruction of a people so wretchedly degenerated, and he would have his family provide, that, if they could not <hi type="italic">in the peace thereof,</hi> yet even in the midst of the troubles thereof, <hi type="italic">they might have peace.</hi> Let them therefore have little to lose, and then losing times would be the less dreadful to them: let them sit loose to what they had, and then they might with less pain be stripped of it. Note, Those are in the best frame to meet sufferings who are mortified to the world and live a life of self-denial. (6.) That in general they might learn to live by rule and under discipline. It is good for us all to do so, and to teach our children to do so. Those that have lived long, as Jonadab probably had done when he left this charge to his posterity, can speak by experience of the vanity of the world and the dangerous snares that are in the abundance of its wealth and pleasures, and therefore ought to be regarded when they warn those that come after them to stand upon their guard. <div eID="gen17969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17970" type="x-p"/> II. How strictly his posterity observed these rules, <reference osisRef="Jer.35.8-Jer.35.10">v. 8-10</reference>. They had in their respective generations all of them <hi type="italic">obeyed the voice of Jonadab their father,</hi> had <hi type="italic">done according to all that he commanded them.</hi> They <hi type="italic">drank no wine,</hi> though they dwelt in a country where was plenty of it; their wives and children drank no wine, for those that are temperate themselves should take care that all under their charge should be so too. They built no houses, tilled no ground, but lived upon the products of their cattle. This they did partly in obedience to their ancestor, and out of a veneration they had for his name and authority, and partly from the experience they themselves had of the benefit of living such a mortified life. See the force of tradition, and the influence that antiquity, example, and great names, have upon men, and how that which seems very difficult will by long usage and custom become easy and in a manner natural. Now, 1. As to one of the particulars he had given them in charge, we are here told how in a case of necessity they dispensed with the violation of it (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">When the king of Babylon came into the land</hi> with his army, though they had hitherto dwelt in tents, they now quitted their tents, and came and dwelt in Jerusalem, and in such houses as they could furnish themselves with there. Note, The rules of a strict discipline must not be made too strict, but so as to admit of a dispensation when the necessity of a case calls for it, which therefore, in making vows of that nature, it is wisdom to provide expressly for, that the way may be made the more clear, and we may not afterwards be forced to say, <hi type="italic">It was an error,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.6">Eccles. v. 6</reference>. Commands of that nature are to be understood with such limitations. These Rechabites would have tempted God, and not trusted him, if they had not used proper means for their own safety in a time of common calamity, notwithstanding the law and custom of their family. 2. As to the other particular, we are here told how, notwithstanding the greatest urgency, they religiously adhered to it. Jeremiah took them into the temple (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.2">v. 2</reference>), into a <hi type="italic">prophet's chamber,</hi> there, rather than into the <hi type="italic">chamber of the princes,</hi> that joined to it, because he had a message from God, which would look more like itself when it was delivered in the <hi type="italic">chambers of a man of God.</hi> There he not only asked the Rechabites whether they would drink any wine, but he set <hi type="italic">pots full of wine before them,</hi> and cups to drink out of, made the temptation as strong as possible, and said, "<hi type="italic">Drink you wine,</hi> you shall have it on free cost. You have broken one of the rules of your order, in coming to live at Jerusalem; why may you not break this too, and when you are in the city do as they there do?" But they peremptorily refused. They all agreed in the refusal. "No, <hi type="italic">we will drink no wine;</hi> for with us it is against the law." The prophet knew very well they would deny it, and, when they did, urged it no further, for he saw they were stedfastly resolved. Note, Those temptations are of no force with men of confirmed sobriety which yet daily overcome such as, notwithstanding their convictions, are of no resolution in the paths of virtue.
entries.432b076cbc9214d2a8edb4e8cb088a289288ea58: <div eID="gen17970" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Case of the Rechabites Applied. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 607.)</title> <div sID="gen17971" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Then came the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto Jeremiah, saying, <hi type="super">13</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel; Go and tell the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, Will ye not receive instruction to hearken to my words? saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">14</hi> The words of Jonadab the son of Rechab, that he commanded his sons not to drink wine, are performed; for unto this day they drink none, but obey their father's commandment: notwithstanding I have spoken unto you, rising early and speaking; but ye hearkened not unto me. <hi type="super">15</hi> I have sent also unto you all my servants the prophets, rising up early and sending <hi type="italic">them,</hi> saying, Return ye now every man from his evil way, and amend your doings, and go not after other gods to serve them, and ye shall dwell in the land which I have given to you and to your fathers: but ye have not inclined your ear, nor hearkened unto me. <hi type="super">16</hi> Because the sons of Jonadab the son of Rechab have performed the commandment of their father, which he commanded them; but this people hath not hearkened unto me: <hi type="super">17</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of hosts, the God of Israel; Behold, I will bring upon Judah and upon all the inhabitants of Jerusalem all the evil that I have pronounced against them: because I have spoken unto them, but they have not heard; and I have called unto them, but they have not answered. <hi type="super">18</hi> And Jeremiah said unto the house of the Rechabites, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel; Because ye have obeyed the commandment of Jonadab your father, and kept all his precepts, and done according unto all that he hath commanded you: <hi type="super">19</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, the God of Israel; Jonadab the son of Rechab shall not want a man to stand before me for ever. <div eID="gen17971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17972" type="x-p"/> The trial of the Rechabites' constancy was intended but for a sign; now here we have the application of it. <div eID="gen17972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17973" type="x-p"/> I. The Rechabites' observance of their father's charge to them is made use of as an aggravation of the disobedience of the Jews to God. Let them see it and be ashamed. The prophet asks them, in God's name, "<hi type="italic">Will you not</hi> at length <hi type="italic">receive instruction?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.35.13">v. 13</reference>. Will nothing affect you? Will nothing fasten upon you? Will nothing prevail to discover sin and duty to you? You see how obedient the Rechabites are to their father's commandment (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.14">v. 14</reference>); but <hi type="italic">you have not inclined your ear to me</hi>" (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.15">v. 15</reference>), though one might much more reasonably expect that the people of God should have obeyed him than that the sons of Jonadab should have obeyed him; and the aggravation is very high, for, 1. The Rechabites were obedient to one who was but a man like themselves, who had but the wisdom and power of a man, and was only the father of their flesh; but the Jews were disobedient to an infinite and eternal God, who had an absolute authority over them, as the Father of their spirits. 2. Jonadab was long since dead, and was ignorant of them, and could neither take cognizance of their disobedience to his orders nor give correction for it; but God lives for ever, to see how his laws are observed, and is in a readiness to revenge all disobedience. 3. The Rechabites were never put in mind of their obligations to their father; but God often sent his prophets to his people, to put them in mind of their duty to him, and yet they would not do it. This is insisted on here as a great aggravation of their disobedience: "<hi type="italic">I have</hi> myself <hi type="italic">spoken to you, rising early and speaking</hi> by the written word and the dictates and admonitions of conscience (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.14">v. 14</reference>); nay, <hi type="italic">I have sent unto you all my servants the prophets,</hi> men like yourselves, whose terrors shall not make you afraid, <hi type="italic">rising up early and sending them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.15">v. 15</reference>), and yet all in vain." 4. Jonadab never did that for his seed which God had done for his people. He left them a charge, but left them no estate to bear the charge; but God had given his people a <hi type="italic">good land,</hi> and promised them that, if they would be obedient, they should still dwell in it, so that they were bound both in gratitude and interest to be obedient, and yet they <hi type="italic">would not hear,</hi> they would not <hi type="italic">hearken.</hi> 5. God did not tie up his people to so much hardship, and to such instances of mortification, as Jonadab obliged his seed to; and yet Jonadab's orders were obeyed and God's were not. <div eID="gen17973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17974" type="x-p"/> II. Judgments are threatened, as often before, against Judah and Jerusalem, for their disobedience thus aggravated. The Rechabites shall rise up in judgment against them, and shall condemn them; for they very punctually <hi type="italic">performed the commandment of their father,</hi> and continued and persevered in their obedience to it (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.16">v. 16</reference>); but <hi type="italic">this people,</hi> this rebellious and gainsaying people, <hi type="italic">have not hearkened unto me;</hi> and therefore (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.17">v. 17</reference>), because they have not obeyed the precepts of the word, God will perform the threatenings of it: "<hi type="italic">I will bring upon them,</hi> by the Chaldean army, <hi type="italic">all the evil pronounced against them</hi> both in the law and in the prophets, for <hi type="italic">I have spoken to them, I have called to them</hi>—spoken in a still small voice to those that were near and called aloud to those that were at a distance, tried all ways and means to convince and reduce them—spoken by my word, called by my providence, both to the same purport, and yet all to no purpose; they have not <hi type="italic">heard</hi> nor <hi type="italic">answered.</hi>" <div eID="gen17974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17975" type="x-p"/> III. Mercy is here promised to the family of the Rechabites for their steady and unanimous adherence to the laws of their house. Though it was only for the shaming of Israel that their constancy was tried, yet, being unshaken, it was <hi type="italic">found unto praise, and honour, and glory;</hi> and God takes occasion from it to tell them that he had favours in reserve for them (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.18-Jer.35.19">v. 18, 19</reference>) and that they should have the comfort of them. 1. That the family shall continue as long as any of the families of Israel, among whom they were strangers and sojourners. it shall <hi type="italic">never want a man</hi> to inherit what they had, though they had no inheritance to leave. Note, Sometimes those that have the smallest estates have the most numerous progeny; but he that sends mouths will be sure to send meat. 2. That religion shall continue in the family: "<hi type="italic">He shall not want a man to stand before me,</hi> to serve me." Though they are neither priests nor levites, nor appear to have had any post in the temple service, yet in a constant course of regular devotion, they stand before God, to minister to him. Note, (1.) The greatest blessing that can be entailed upon a family is to have the worship of God kept up in it from generation to generation. (2.) Temperance, self-denial, and mortification to the world, do very much befriend the exercises of piety, and help to transmit the observance of them to posterity. The more dead we are to the delights of sense the better we are disposed for the service of God; but nothing is more fatal to the entail of religion in a family than pride and luxury.  <chapter eID="Jer.35"/> <div eID="gen17975" type="x-p"/>

entries.f832ab16f806bfcd8e19b0ca365fb7739e6af8e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10371"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 35</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.35.1-Jer.35.19">Jr 35:1-19</reference>. Prophecy in the Reign of Jehoiakim, when the Chaldeans, in Conjunction with the Syrians and Moabites, Invaded Judea.</title> <div sID="gen18501" type="x-p"/> By the obedience of the Rechabites to their father, Jeremiah condemns the disobedience of the Jews to God their Father. The Holy Spirit has arranged Jeremiah's prophecies by the moral rather than the chronological connection. From the history of an event fifteen years before, the Jews, who had brought back their manumitted servants into bondage, are taught how much God loves and rewards obedience, and hates and punishes disobedience.<div eID="gen18501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18502" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10371"/><hi type="bold">2. Rechabites--</hi>a nomadic tribe belonging to the Kenites of Hemath (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.55">1Ch 2:55</reference>), of the family of Jethro, or Hobab, Moses' father-in-law (<reference osisRef="Exod.18.9">Ex 18:9</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Num.10.29-Num.10.32">Nu 10:29-32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.1.16">Jud 1:16</reference>). They came into Canaan with the Israelites, but, in order to preserve their independence, chose a life in tents without a fixed habitation (<reference osisRef="1Sam.15.6">1Sa 15:6</reference>). Besides the branch of them associated with Judah and extending to Amalek, there was another section at Kadesh, in Naphtali (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.11">Jud 4:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.17">17</reference>). They seem to have been proselytes of the gate, Jonadab, son of Rechab, whose charge not to drink wine they so strictly obeyed, was zealous for God (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.15-2Kgs.10.23">2Ki 10:15-23</reference>). The Nabatheans of Arabia observed the same rules [Diodorus Siculus, 19.94].<div eID="gen18502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18503" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bring ... into ... house of ... Lord--</hi>because there were suitable witnesses at hand there from among the priests and chief men, as also because he had the power immediately to address the people assembled there (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.13">Jr 35:13</reference>). It may have been also as a reproof of the priests, who drank wine freely, though commanded to refrain from it when in the discharge of their duties [Calvin].<div eID="gen18503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18504" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chambers--</hi>which were round about the temple, applied to various uses, for example, to contain the vestments, sacred vessels, &c. <div eID="gen18504" type="x-p"/>

entries.0250ea05ce6b32471643e995191302decfccc4a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10373"/><div sID="gen18506" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10373"/><hi type="bold">4. man of God--</hi>a prophet (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.1">De 33:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.27">1Sa 2:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.22">1Ki 12:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.7">2Ki 4:7</reference>), also "a servant of God" in general (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.11">1Ti 6:11</reference>), one not his own, but God's; one who has parted with all right in himself to give himself wholly to God (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.17">2Ti 3:17</reference>). He was so reverenced that none would call in question what was transacted in his chamber.<div eID="gen18506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">keeper of the door--</hi>Hebrew, "of the vessel." Probably the office meant is that of the priest who kept in charge the capitation money paid for the use of the temple and the votive offerings, such as silver vessels, &c. There were seven such keepers [Grotius]. Compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.12.9">2Ki 12:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.18">25:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.18">1Ch 9:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.19">19</reference>, which support English Version.<div eID="gen18507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I said ... Drink--</hi>Jeremiah does not say, The Lord saith, Drink: for then they would have been bound to obey. Contrast the case in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.7-1Kgs.13.26">1Ki 13:7-26</reference>. <div eID="gen18508" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8ffbaa7a92af0fac35de1a67e40b4c389cb5de6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10374"/><div sID="gen18509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10374"/><hi type="bold">6. Jonadab ... our father--</hi>that is, forefather and director, three hundred years before (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.15">2Ki 10:15</reference>). They were called Rechabites, not Jonadabites, having received their name from Rechab the father, previously to their adopting the injunctions of Jonadab his son. This case affords no justification for slavish deference to the religious opinions of the Christian fathers: for Jonadab's injunction only affected matters of the present life; moreover, it was not binding on their consciences, for they deemed it not unlawful to go to Jerusalem in the invasion (<reference osisRef="Jer.35.11">Jr 35:11</reference>). What is praised here is not the father's injunction, but the obedience of the sons [Calvin]. <div eID="gen18509" type="x-p"/>
entries.b0d1bc4e2d507de6ede6c23b0d5970ff1ce85434: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10375"/><div sID="gen18510" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10375"/><hi type="bold">7. tents--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Judg.4.17">Jud 4:17</reference>).<div eID="gen18510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18511" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">live many days--</hi>according to the promise connected with the fifth commandment (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.12">Ex 20:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.2">Ep 6:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.3">3</reference>).<div eID="gen18511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strangers--</hi>They were not of the stock of Jacob, but sojourners in Israel. Types of the children of God, pilgrims on earth, looking for heaven as their home: having little to lose, so that losing times cost them little alarm; sitting loose to what they have (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.34">He 10:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.9">11:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.13-Heb.10.16">10, 13-16</reference>). <div eID="gen18512" type="x-p"/>
entries.c4c90fab26497be72230491ba26fb7a70baae3ac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10376"/><div sID="gen18513" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10376"/><hi type="bold">8. all that he ... charged us ... all our days, we ... wives ... sons ... daughters--</hi>unreserved obedience in all particulars, at all times, and on the part of all, without exception: in these respects Israel's obedience to God was wanting. Contrast <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.20">1Sa 15:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.21">21</reference>; Psa 78:34-37, 41, 56, 57. <div eID="gen18513" type="x-p"/>
entries.babeb0776b75ec2e4e0dde5989796a240a2448ac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10377"/><div sID="gen18514" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10377"/><hi type="bold">11. Chaldeans ... Syrians--</hi>when Jehoiakim revolted from Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.1">2Ki 24:1</reference>, 2). Necessity sets aside all other laws. This is the Rechabites' excuse for their seeming disobedience to Jonadab in temporarily settling in a city. Herein was seen the prescient wisdom of Jonadab's commands; they could at a moment's notice migrate, having no land possessions to tie them. <div eID="gen18514" type="x-p"/>
entries.5299e3e13331f74a28ea69e4c4db719ffe510a90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10378"/><div sID="gen18515" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10378"/><hi type="bold">14. obey ... father's commandment: notwithstanding I--</hi>(Mal 1:6).<div eID="gen18515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18516" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rising early and speaking--</hi>God Himself speaking late and early by His various ways of providence and grace. <div eID="gen18516" type="x-p"/>
entries.69d828de49523b97e60b98e5adef31422b4688d1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10379"/><div sID="gen18517" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10379"/>15. In <reference osisRef="Jer.35.15">Jr 35:15</reference> and in <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.15">2Ch 36:15</reference>, a distinct mode of address is alluded to, namely, God sending His servants. (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.11">Jr 18:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.5">25:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.6">6</reference>). I enjoined nothing unreasonable, but simply to serve Me, and I attached to the command a gracious promise, but in vain. If Jonadab's commands, which were arbitrary and not moral obligations in themselves, were obeyed, much more ought Mine, which are in themselves right. <div eID="gen18517" type="x-p"/>
entries.761c13de9c8551c62bb0b7e775f82ec5d876772a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10380"/><div sID="gen18518" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10380"/><hi type="bold">17. because I have spoken ... not heard ...
